author: reek
body: Rings are the real discipline, not a shortcut: every producer ring (command, endpoint zero, each bulk endpoint) carries its enqueue index and producer cycle state in a small header before the TRB array, ends in a pre-written link TRB with the toggle-cycle flag, and wraps by activating that link and flipping its cycle. A real controller caches ring position from the moment Address Device or Configure Endpoint reads it out of the input context -- rewinding a dequeue pointer behind its back is not a thing hardware permits, so the driver never does it. Consumed events are acknowledged by writing ERDP back, which real controllers require to know the ring is not full.

author: reek
body: A halted endpoint is restarted by pointing the controller back at the ring, and the only position it may be given is one the producer has not yet filled: the current enqueue slot, carrying the producer's own cycle state as the dequeue cycle. Anything behind that is a TRB the controller has already consumed, and anything ahead of it is not written yet.

author: reek
body: The route string is what says WHERE a device is. Without it a device addressed through two tiers of hub is indistinguishable from one on a root port, because every other field is the same -- the root port it descends from, its speed, its slot. A hub walk that cannot report where it arrived cannot be checked by anything.

author: reek
body: The transaction translator is carried on the device for the same reason. A full-speed device reaches a high-speed bus only through some ancestor hub's translator, and that ancestor is not always the hub it is plugged into -- a full-speed hub has none of its own and passes its parent's along. Recording which translator serves this device is what lets its children inherit the right one.

author: reek
body: On real metal there is no serial log, so the bring-up records what it found -- controller identity, capability parameters, the ownership handoff, and a raw snapshot of every root port the instant the controller starts -- into a fixed cell block that a later screen reads. The magic dword is written LAST so a partial capture (a bring-up that faulted midway) is never mistaken for a complete one; the field that never got written names how far the bring-up got.

author: reek
body: 48 upwards is four dwords per controller for the first four: identity, location, outcome, and what was found there. The outcome is three-valued for the reason index 30 is -- 0 "never reached" must not read the same as 1 "opened, bring-up failed" or 2 "running and walked".

author: reek
body: 64-69 are the boot keyboard's interrupt endpoint, and they exist to be a COMPARISON: what the device's descriptor asked for beside what we programmed into its endpoint context. A value alone is satisfied by any plausible number, so a mismatch is the finding and a lone reading is not. 64 is three-valued for the same reason 30 and the outcome above are: a bInterval of zero because the descriptor was never fetched must not read the same as a bInterval genuinely zero.

author: reek
body: 70-74 are the mass-storage bring-up ladder, owned by GopUsbMsc: the furthest rung reached, the Configure Endpoint completion code, the block size the medium reported, the sector count, and the bConfigurationValue the driver sent. They are three-valued in the same way -- a zero rung is a bring-up that never reached the first one, and there is no completion code zero for the second cell to collide with.

author: reek
body: 74 is written BEFORE the request it describes is issued, which is the point of it: a refused SET_CONFIGURATION has to be able to show the value that was refused, or the reading cannot tell a wrong value from a device that refuses every value.

author: reek
body: 75-78 say WHERE the mass-storage device was and what actually came back from its SET_CONFIGURATION: controller ordinal plus one, port, speed and slot packed a byte each, then the route string, then the completion code, then that port's own PORTSC. The code is the point -- a STALL, a Transaction Error and the fuel expiring are three different faults and the Boolean rendered them as one. The PORTSC is taken AT THE DEVICE rather than left to the snapshot, which covers eight ports on a controller that may have twenty-six.

author: reek
body: 46 is a bitmask of which root ports report a device connected, one bit per port up to 32. Index 18 counts them, and a count names none of them: the ASUS answered connected=4 with the device that mattered on port 9, which no snapshot row reaches.

author: reek
body: 79 is the completion code of a SECOND SET_CONFIGURATION, asked only when the first was refused and never acted on. A transient failure and a permanent one want opposite fixes and one attempt cannot tell them apart; the cell turns "a retry might help" from a guess into a measurement, at the cost of one idempotent request.

author: reek
body: The ordinal of the controller currently being walked, plus one. Indices 0 to 39 are restored from the snapshot taken when the keyboard was credited, so on a two-controller machine they describe the KEYBOARD's controller and a device found on the other one has nothing on screen naming where it was. 45 is written as each controller's walk begins, so anything recorded during that walk can say which one it happened on.

author: reek
body: The status goes in LAST, so a bring-up that faults midway leaves it zero and the reading says the fields were never taken rather than showing the residue of whatever the firmware left.

author: reek
body: Which controller 0-39 describe is not a presentation question. The handback in KbdDiagProbe computes the capability base as the KEYBOARD host's operational base minus cell 4, then scans from there for the legacy-support capability using cell 8 and writes cell 39 back into it. On a machine with one controller those agree by accident. On a machine with two they name different controllers, and the handback then walks a capability list at an address derived from mismatched halves.

author: reek
body: So the walk keeps a copy of 0-39 taken at the moment the keyboard is credited and puts it back once every controller is up. A copy is exact where a re-read is not: cell 39 is the firmware's pre-handoff control word and 20-27 are the port snapshot taken the instant the controller started, and neither exists to be read a second time.

author: reek
body: A controller must be halted before it is reset: resetting a running controller is undefined. Clear Run/Stop and wait for HCHalted; a controller firmware already stopped answers at once.

author: reek
body: A device behind a hub gets its speed from the hub's port status, which has no PSI value in it at all, so the encode is a reverse lookup by rate rather than a pass-through of what PORTSC said. Where no declared PSI dword carries the class, the class itself is written: that is a controller whose vocabulary cannot express the device, and it is what this driver did before it read PSI dwords at all, so it is a guess that is no worse rather than a new refusal.

author: reek
body: The reverse of the handoff, and the reason it exists: on a board whose firmware presents its USB keyboard as a PS/2 one through an SMM legacy handler, taking ownership by the book DISABLES that emulation. If the pure USB path then fails to deliver a keystroke, the machine has no keyboard at all -- and that is exactly what happened here on real hardware: the working path was scuttled in the same change that introduced its replacement, and the replacement did not hold weight.

author: reek
body: So the cord goes back. Halt the controller, so firmware inherits a quiescent device rather than a running one; restore the SMI enables the firmware itself had chosen, verbatim, from the word saved at the handoff; clear the OS-owned semaphore; and watch for BIOS-owned to return. A firmware may take a measurable stretch of SMM work to re-own a controller, so the wait is fuel-bounded and its outcome is recorded rather than asserted -- a board that never re-owns says so at index 29 instead of hanging.

author: reek
body: What this costs, stated plainly: the controller is shared, so a USB mass-storage boot stick dies with the keyboard's endpoint. The caller must therefore only reach for this when there is no keyboard at all, which is a machine that cannot be driven anyway. A keyboard and no stick beats a stick and no keyboard.

author: reek
body: A raw PORTSC snapshot of the root ports the moment the controller runs, plus a count of ports reporting a device connected. This is the single most telling line on a board that enumerates nothing: all-zero connect bits point at port power or chipset routing, live connect bits at the enumeration path above.

author: reek
body: QEMU could not show it and the reason is not that it zeroes RAM. Its controller reports exactly EIGHT ports, so the write lands on the last legal cell and stops. The bed sat precisely on the boundary.

author: reek
body: The bound is the cell count, not a second literal, so the two cannot drift apart again. Ports at or above the bound are still COUNTED -- the connected total is the number the enumeration path is judged against and it must cover every port, which is how a device on port 9 shows up in `connected=` while having no PORTSC row of its own.

author: reek
body: A COUNT of connected ports names none of them, and on a controller wider than the eight rows above it that is the difference between a reading and a rumour: the ASUS answered connected=4 while the device that mattered sat on port 9, which no row could show. One bit per port, up to 32, says WHICH -- and it is the only place a port above the snapshot band appears at all.

author: reek
body: Wait n PIT ticks, exiting the instant the counter has advanced far enough. If the tick never moves -- an environment where the timer interrupt is not delivered -- the fuel bounds a busy spin so timing alone can never hang the boot.

author: reek
body: Set Port Power on every root port. PORTSC carries write-1-to-clear change bits, so the write names only the intent -- Port Power alone -- and never echoes the read value back, the same discipline the reset path follows. Harmless on a controller that powers its ports unconditionally.

author: reek
body: The claim that QEMU "zeroes its RAM and could not fail this" was true of the wrong mechanism. Its controller reports exactly eight ports, so the overrun lands on the last legal cell. The bed sat on the boundary.

author: reek
body: The scan is taken once and handed in. `pci-scan-all` walks the bridge tree and allocates as it goes, and there is no collector, so a caller that re-scanned per controller would pay for the whole tree again on every round.

author: reek
body: So the test is membership of the device window, not the height of one dword. A BAR is used where it lies only when it is memory, non-zero, 32-bit-addressable and inside [3 GB, 4 GB); everything else relocates, which this driver can do and a NIC driver cannot. The verdict and the address it judged are recorded, because a board that lands somewhere unexpected should say so rather than be inferred from a dead screen.

author: reek
body: Some controllers demand private scratchpad pages: HCSPARAMS2 states how many, and slot zero of the device context array must point at an array of that many page pointers before Run. A controller that asks and is not answered corrupts memory it was never given.

author: reek
body: The controller produces events; the driver consumes them at its own dequeue index, accepting a TRB only when its cycle bit matches the driver's cycle state, flipping that state each time the index wraps. Each consumed event is acknowledged by writing ERDP back with the event-handler-busy bit, which is how a real controller learns the ring has room.

author: reek
body: One command TRB, doorbell zero, then wait for the command completion event. Completion code 1 is success.

author: reek
body: The controller learns about a device only through input contexts: Address Device reads the slot and endpoint-zero contexts, Configure Endpoint the slot and each added endpoint. Root-hub port numbers are one-based. Endpoint types in context encoding: control 4, bulk OUT 2, bulk IN 6, interrupt IN 7. The dequeue pointer carries the ring's cycle state in bit zero; error-count three is the conventional bulk/control retry budget.

author: reek
body: A device behind a hub is named by the route string in slot-context dword zero, bits 19:0: one nibble per tier, each the one-based downstream port number of the hub at that tier, with the root port kept separately in dword one. A device on a root port has route zero. A low- or full-speed device below a HIGH-speed hub needs that hub's transaction translator: dword two names the parent hub's slot and the parent port, and the controller issues split transactions through them. Below a full-speed hub the whole chain runs at one speed and the fields stay zero.

author: reek
body: Every context is ctxsz bytes -- 32 on a controller reporting CSZ=0 (QEMU), 64 on most real Intel silicon (CSZ=1). The input control context sits at offset 0; the slot context at one context size; the endpoint contexts follow, endpoint-zero (device context index 1) at two context sizes. Writing the slot context at a hardcoded 32 on a 64-byte controller lands it inside the input control context, and Address Device then reads a garbage slot -- a device that resets and connects but never addresses. A 64-byte input context with a high device-context index reaches 33 contexts, so the buffer is sized for that ceiling.

author: reek
body: The single-endpoint variant, for a device whose interesting traffic is one interrupt endpoint: a HID keyboard's reports.

author: reek
body: Enable Slot returns the slot id in the completion event. The output device context handed to the controller through DCBAA is the controller's own memory from then on; the driver initializes the endpoint-zero dequeue there once for device models that read it directly (codex-vm) and never touches it again -- real controllers take ring positions only from input contexts.

author: reek
body: The output device context follows the same size, but with no input control context ahead of it: the slot context is at offset zero and endpoint context d at d context sizes.

author: reek
body: A device that refuses a command answers its bulk endpoint with STALL (completion code 6), and the endpoint stops there: the controller puts it in the Halted state and every later doorbell on it is ignored. Two halves have to be undone, and doing either alone leaves a pipe that looks recovered and moves nothing.

author: reek
body: The controller half is Reset Endpoint, which takes the endpoint out of Halted, followed by Set TR Dequeue Pointer -- mandatory after a reset, because the controller's saved position is the TRB that stalled and it will not resume past it on its own. The device half is CLEAR_FEATURE ENDPOINT_HALT on endpoint zero, which clears the condition and resets the data toggle at the far end; skip it and the device stalls again on the next packet.

author: reek
body: The endpoint address the device wants is not the device context index the controller wants: the DCI is the endpoint number doubled, plus one for an IN endpoint, while the wire address is the number with bit seven set for IN.

author: reek
body: The default control pipe recovers with the HOST half only, and the function above must not be used for it. Its last step is CLEAR_FEATURE ENDPOINT_HALT, which is a control transfer -- on endpoint zero that request would have to travel through the very pipe it is recovering. USB 2.0 8.5.3.4 also makes it unnecessary: a control endpoint's halt is cleared by the next SETUP, which a device is required to accept even while halted, so there is no device half to clear.

author: reek
body: A control transfer is three TRBs on the endpoint-zero ring: SETUP with the eight setup bytes immediate in the parameter dwords, DATA pointing at the buffer, STATUS closing the handshake in the opposite direction of the data. Only the status TRB carries IOC, so exactly one transfer event answers the whole transfer; a short data stage is normal (a descriptor read asks for more than most descriptors hold) and ends the data TD silently.

author: reek
body: The completion code is the diagnosis and the Boolean throws it away. A STALL is the device refusing a request it understood, a Transaction Error is the wire, and the fuel running out is neither -- three different next steps rendered as one `False`. Callers that only branch keep the Boolean; a caller standing at a failure it has to explain takes the code.
